The reaction shown is: CaC2 + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + C2H2 (acetylene)

When acetylene (C2H2) comes into contact with copper, it can form copper acetylides (Cu2C2). Copper acetylides are known to be highly explosive compounds, especially when dry. This is why copper and copper alloys (like brass) are strictly avoided in equipment used for handling acetylene.

The explosive nature of copper acetylides is well-established in chemistry safety protocols. This is why acetylene equipment (tanks, regulators, etc.) is specifically made without copper components.

Looking at the options:
A. Copper catalyzes the decomposition of acetylene - This happens but is not the primary concern
B. Copper forms explosive acetylides - This is the main safety concern
C. Copper increases the flammability of acetylene - Not the primary issue
D. Copper reduces the purity of acetylene - Not the main concern
E. The reaction will take place normally - This is incorrect given the safety hazard

Based on this analysis, the correct answer is B. Copper forms explosive acetylides.
